title: The U.S. banned Nvidia's best chips from going to China. Now it's trying to close a crucial loophole
gist: CNBC details how Chinese AI firms including Moonshot, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent are reportedly accessing Nvidia's most advanced chips' compute power via cloud data centers in Thailand, Malaysia and Japan, exploiting a loophole where US export controls restrict chip ownership but not remote access, with a bill (RASA) to close it stalled in the Senate.

insights.claim: Nvidia's most advanced AI chips, including GB300s, are banned from direct export to China, but several Chinese firms have reportedly accessed the chips' compute power via data centers in Southeast Asia.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Shows that a hardware export ban is not equivalent to denying China frontier AI training capacity, meaning current export-control effectiveness against China's AI buildout is overstated.
insights.locator: despite U.S. restrictions on exporting the company's most advanced semiconductors

insights.claim: The US export-control regime targets physical ownership of AI chips, not remote or cloud-based access to their compute power, according to Cassia King of the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy.
insights.speaker: Cassia King (Institute for AI Policy and Strategy), via Kai Nicol-Schwarz
entities: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy
insights.so_what: Defines the precise regulatory gap that cloud-compute arbitrage exploits, a key variable for handicapping how fast the US can close it via new rulemaking.
insights.quote: controls physical AI chips. It does not cover remote access to those chips.
insights.locator: She said the U.S. export control regime

insights.claim: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 model, released in July, was accused by White House official Michael Kratsios of being trained using Nvidia GB300 chips accessed via a facility in Thailand.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: A concrete, named case tying a specific frontier Chinese model release to alleged loophole use, which could become the political trigger for tighter US rules.
insights.locator: Less than a week after Moonshot AI released a new model in July

insights.claim: Kimi K3 is one of a wave of new Chinese AI models (alongside recent releases from DeepSeek and Alibaba) making rapid performance leaps as the US-China AI race intensifies, and industry watchers say access to overseas cloud compute is a key factor behind Chinese models' gains.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Directly ties Chinese frontier-model performance gains to offshore compute access, making the loophole a real lever for slowing (or the loophole's persistence a driver of) Chinese AI progress.
insights.locator: Industry watchers say access to advanced compute via overseas cloud providers

insights.claim: Moonshot's reported compute access via a Thai facility is legal so long as the company is not directly buying and owning the physical Nvidia hardware itself, according to Cassia King.
insights.speaker: Cassia King (Institute for AI Policy and Strategy), via Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Clarifies that current offshore-compute activity, while eroding sanctions intent, is not necessarily illegal today, constraining near-term enforcement absent new legislation.
insights.quote: so long as Moonshot isn't actually buying and owning the physical hardware directly.
insights.locator: told CNBC that Moonshot's reported access to compute

themes.theme: Scale of Chinese Hyperscaler Offshore Compute Access

insights.claim: Chinese hyperscalers ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have reportedly accessed Nvidia compute power remotely via data centers in Thailand, Malaysia and Japan.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Indicates this is a systematic offshore-compute strategy used by China's largest tech firms, not a one-off case, sizing the scope of the loophole's use.
insights.locator: Chinese hyperscalers including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent

insights.claim: ByteDance was reportedly working with Singapore-headquartered cloud provider Aolani to access Nvidia compute in Malaysia (first reported by the Wall Street Journal in March); Aolani says its customers have no ownership or physical access to the underlying chips and that its services are fully compliant with applicable regulations.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Names a specific intermediary cloud-provider structure that regulators and investors could scrutinize as a template for compliant-but-loophole-exploiting arrangements.
insights.quote: The companies we service do not have ownership, potential future claim or physical access to the chips that power our solutions.
insights.locator: ByteDance was working with Singapore-headquartered Aolani

insights.claim: AI infrastructure buildouts in Southeast Asia are booming: JLL estimates global data center capacity could roughly double to 200GW by 2030, and DC Byte data shows 31 planned 100MW+ data centers across Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand versus just two today.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Quantifies a massive regional data-center capex wave partly enabling this compute-arbitrage dynamic, an investable regional infrastructure theme (power, land, connectivity) regardless of the export-control outcome.
insights.locator: Real estate company JLL estimates that global data center capacity

themes.theme: The Legislative Fix: Remote Access Security Act

insights.claim: Michelle Nie of CNAS calls the remote-access loophole a threat to national security, arguing that 'the point of chip export controls is to deny China the ability to train frontier AI using advanced U.S. chips.'
insights.speaker: Michelle Nie (CNAS), via Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Frames the loophole as an active undermining of the strategic intent behind export controls, a rationale likely to drive further legislative/regulatory action.
insights.quote: The point of chip export controls is to deny China the ability to train frontier AI using advanced U.S. chips.
insights.locator: Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow in technology and national security

insights.claim: The Remote Access Security Act (RASA) would expand US export controls to cover remote cloud-based access to controlled hardware and software; it passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate.
insights.speaker: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: A key regulatory catalyst and timing risk for cloud providers and Chinese AI firms relying on offshore Nvidia compute; Senate passage would be a material event for the sector.
insights.locator: A proposed piece of legislation, the Remote Access Security Act

insights.claim: RASA faces potential industry pushback because cloud providers would bear the compliance burden of any know-your-customer (KYC) and customer-verification requirements the bill mandates.
insights.speaker: Michelle Nie (CNAS), via Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Cloud/hyperscaler lobbying is a headwind to Senate passage, a factor to weigh when handicapping the bill's timeline.
insights.quote: Cloud providers would bear the compliance burden of any KYC and customer verification requirements mandated by the bill.
insights.locator: It faces potential industry pushback, Nie said

insights.claim: Passing RASA alone would not solve the problem: it would only give the US government authority to regulate remote access, and a separate implementing rule would still be needed to actually export-control that access.
insights.speaker: Michelle Nie (CNAS), via Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Implies a two-step regulatory process and a longer lag before the loophole is actually closed even after legislative passage, relevant to compliance and enforcement timing.
insights.locator: The passing of RASA alone wouldn't solve the problem

insights.claim: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) could push through an implementing rule 'in a matter of days' with White House support, according to Cassia King, though designing an effective, enforceable rule (defining covered compute, prohibited users, and a robust KYC scheme) remains the real challenge.
insights.speaker: Cassia King (Institute for AI Policy and Strategy), via Kai Nicol-Schwarz
insights.so_what: Signals the loophole could be closed quickly and with little warning if the administration prioritizes it, sharply curtailing Chinese hyperscalers' offshore-compute workaround.
insights.quote: The challenge will be in making a rule that's effective and enforceable.
insights.locator: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) could push through a rule quickly
